title: MongoDB is a Leader in The Forrester Wave™: Translytical Data Platforms
summary:
We’re pleased to announce that MongoDB has been recognized as a Leader in the recently released Forrester Wave™: Translytical Data Platforms, Q4 2024.

The report—which highlights “Leaders, Strong Performers, Contenders, and Challengers” and is “an assessment of the top vendors in the market”—notes that “MongoDB is an excellent choice for organizations looking to enhance their document and NoSQL platforms with real-time insights by leveraging translytical capabilities.”

What are translytical capabilities?

So what are translytical capabilities? In short, modern applications use a growing number of data types for transactional, operational, and analytical uses. Developers can silo different data types and workloads into separate systems, but this causes architectural complexity and reduced agility for teams.

A better approach—and one that speeds development—is to leverage a single platform that can store and use multiple data types for different purposes. Forrester defines these “translytical data platforms” as “next-generation data solutions built on a single database engine to seamlessly support transactional, operational, and analytical workloads without compromising data integrity, performance, or real-time analytics.”

That’s why we built MongoDB Atlas as a modern database. It brings data like documents, vectors, streaming, and time-series together in one system so that you can run transactional, operational, and analytics workloads in one place.

How Forrester measured translytical capabilities

To measure providers, Forrester evaluated 15 of the most significant translytical data platform vendors against 26 criteria. These criteria span current offering and strategy, to market presence. Being recognized as a Leader is based on an organization’s scores in both current offering and strategy categories for criteria like vision and innovation.

Forrester gave MongoDB the highest possible scores across nine criteria, including:

  • Multimodel1

  • Search

  • Development Tools / API

  • Scale optimization

  • Streaming

  • Platform management

  • Roadmap

  • Adoption

  • Number of customers

According to the report, “MongoDB continues to expand its translytical market share by delivering new capabilities that enhance automation, intelligent memory tiering, and multimodel support, including vector, streaming, analytics, and integrated transactions.”

“Developers have been telling us for years that they need easy ways to work with all their data in one place,” said Jim Scharf, Chief Technology Officer at MongoDB. “That’s what continues to drive our strategy of making MongoDB Atlas the modern database. We’re excited to be recognized as a Leader in the new The Forrester Wave™: Translytical Data Platforms, and we will continue to support our customers’ growing needs for their data.”

What are MongoDB customers doing with translytical capabilities?

The Forrester report notes that organizations “use MongoDB to support real-time analytics, customer intelligence, the Internet of Things (IoT), and AI applications.” So, let’s look at a few examples in action.

Companies like Ignition started using MongoDB just for operational data—but, over time, expanded into using Atlas Vector Search for AI use cases. Meanwhile, Bosch Digital makes their IoT data easier to work with by bringing multiple data sources together in a single platform. And, Keller Williams uses MongoDB Charts to bring their analytics to where their transactional data is, making it faster to gather insights for their product teams.

Overall, customers are attracted to MongoDB because of how developer-friendly the platform is, and because it simplifies their lives by bringing their data together.

1 Multimodel is defined as support for storing and using various data types.

title: How to Align Modern Payment Platforms with PCI DSS Using MongoDB Enterprise Advanced
summary:
Payment platforms operate in a demanding environment. They must protect payment account data and support the teams that authorize transactions, investigate suspicious activity, and resolve exceptions. The more people and systems that can see sensitive data, the harder it is to control exposure. And the more data is locked away, the harder it can be to use in legitimate workflows. So how can you set up the platforms to ensure they protect that data while also giving the right people access?

Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS), a global security standard managed by the PCI Security Standards Council, provides a framework for protecting payment account data, restricting access, securing networks, and monitoring activity. Meeting those objectives is not a database-only exercise. It depends on how the application handles data, how the database server protects and governs it, and how the underlying infrastructure is configured and operated.

While the fully managed MongoDB Atlas platform can provide a foundation for organizations pursuing PCI DSS compliance, with MongoDB’s infrastructure-level certifications supporting the infrastructure layer, some organizations opt for a self-managed architecture to maintain direct operational control over their infrastructure and internal security policies. For self-managed deployments, MongoDB Enterprise Advanced provides database security, governance, and encryption capabilities that can help support applicable PCI DSS objectives. Red Hat OpenShift provides configurable platform and network controls, while the MongoDB Controllers for Kubernetes (MCK) Operator manages MongoDB deployments on OpenShift.

Achieving alignment across this architecture requires a defense-in-depth model, which provides multiple overlapping layers of cybersecurity to protect data. While technical controls and reference architectures alone do not constitute formal compliance attestations, they provide the foundation needed to meet core PCI DSS objectives. The following sections walk through establishing this foundation across three complementary tiers—application, database, and infrastructure—before examining how they work together to protect sensitive payment workflows.

Start with the application layer

The application determines what payment data enters the platform, where it flows, and which business roles need it. In our reference payment service provider (PSP) demo, the application models two distinct workloads: high-throughput payment authorizations and post-transaction fraud investigations.  

This PSP demo application is designed to support deployment with either a fully managed MongoDB Atlas cluster or a self-managed MongoDB Enterprise Advanced deployment. Its core architecture, data models, and client-side encryption approach can be shared across both models, although configuration, integrations, and operational responsibilities may differ by environment. This dual compatibility gives organizations the flexibility to migrate workloads between cloud and on-premises environments as strategic needs evolve, eliminating infrastructure lock-in. Furthermore, it reinforces data sovereignty by allowing organizations to retain direct operational control over where cardholder data resides and how it is governed across hybrid architectures.

At the functional level, data minimization is enforced at the point of entry. Primary account numbers (PAN) are tokenized when downstream services do not need raw cardholder data, and sensitive authentication data (SAD) such as card verification value (CVV) never gets stored post-authorization. In addition, an isolated application programming interface (API) layer ensures that external clients never connect directly to the database tier.

These design choices reduce unnecessary exposure before data reaches storage. They also make the next layer more effective: The database can apply protection to the fields and workflows that genuinely need it, rather than compensating for an application that collects or shares too much.

Protect and govern data at the database layer

MongoDB Enterprise Advanced provides security capabilities for self-managed MongoDB deployments. One relevant capability is queryable encryption (QE). It allows selected fields to remain encrypted in the database while supporting defined query patterns over those fields. In practical terms, an authorized payment or investigation workflow can look up protected information, such as an account reference, without the database storing that value in plaintext. The client driver encrypts selected fields and decrypts query results using keys from the configured key management service (KMS), meaning the database engine processes only ciphertext for supported query patterns. QE is field- and query-specific, so teams can choose which data must be searchable and validate the supported patterns for their deployment.

Encryption works alongside access governance. MongoDB role-based access control lets administrators assign built-in or custom roles so that application services, analysts, auditors, and database operators receive only the permissions they need. MongoDB also supports IP-based authentication restrictions for database users. These controls help answer two different questions:

  • What may this identity do? 

  • From which network locations may it connect?

Database auditing can complement these protections by recording selected database activity for review and investigation. The value comes from connecting audit policy to the organization’s monitoring and response processes, not simply turning on logging in isolation.

Enforce the environment at the infrastructure layer

The database and application still need a tightly controlled environment. OpenShift provides platform controls that teams can configure to isolate workloads and govern their runtime. Those controls include role-based access for cluster and project operations, security context constraints for pod privileges, and NetworkPolicies to limit which workloads can communicate. For example, a policy can allow the payment API to reach MongoDB while denying unrelated workloads access to the database network path.

The MongoDB controllers for Kubernetes (MCK) operator manages the cluster’s deployment, while Ops Manager provides management capabilities such as automation, monitoring, and backup according to the deployment configuration. These tools help platform and database teams operate the deployment consistently; they do not replace the need to set restrictive policies, manage identities and keys, or review the resulting configuration.

The following high-level view shows how the layers work together:

Figure 1. Payment platform stack, from underlying infrastructure to business applications. 

As shown above, these components align into a defense-in-depth model. The stack builds upward from the host infrastructure and immutable operating system (RHEL OS) to the OpenShift container platform, establishing a hardened foundation. On top of this platform, the MCK operator provides persistence for the encrypted data, Ops Manager orchestrates data automation, and the business payment microservices run isolated at the application tier. This layered view helps teams map controls across each tier to meet PCI DSS requirements.

How the layers support PCI DSS objectives

Application-level tokenization and data minimization can reduce how much sensitive data the platform handles. Queryable encryption can protect selected fields while preserving supported lookup workflows. Database roles and IP restrictions can narrow access to the database, while OpenShift policies can further limit which workloads and network paths reach it. Auditing and operational monitoring help teams review activity and investigate events. The value, ultimately, occurs when this all comes together seamlessly.

As illustrated in Figure 2, the reference PSP demo organizes these controls into clear architectural boundaries:

  • Perimeter and access control: External entities (client devices, wallet systems, and merchant systems) communicate exclusively over HTTPS through the service gateway. Identity and access policies are enforced at the security gateway using standards such as OAuth, OIDC, and JWT backed by general identity and access management (GIAM), preventing direct access to data stores from untrusted networks.

  • Protected core processing: The core system coordinates payment workflows and integrates directly with a key management service (such as AWS KMS) and MongoDB EA. This design ensures that field encryption occurs before persistence and that the database engine handles only ciphertext for configured search patterns.

  • Event decoupling and specialized services: By routing events through an event bus (Kafka) to dedicated providers for fraud detection (FDS) and anti-money laundering (AML), the platform isolates investigative workflows from the core payment engine, supporting workload separation and least-privilege data access.

Figure 2. Reference view of a PCI DSS-aligned payment demo integrated with MongoDB Enterprise Advanced on OpenShift.

Together, these controls can support PCI DSS objectives such as protecting stored account data, restricting access based on business need, maintaining secure network boundaries, and monitoring access. With a self-managed MongoDB EA deployment on OpenShift, the organization remains responsible for the full cardholder data environment, including infrastructure configuration, identity and key management, operational procedures, and evidence.

The payment service demo application makes this layered approach tangible. Its payment and investigation workflows provide concrete context for demonstrating how queryable encryption can protect selected sensitive fields while supporting defined searches, how MongoDB roles and IP-based restrictions narrow database access, and how OpenShift policies can limit paths between the application and data tiers. MCK and the Ops Manager provide deployment and operational tooling for sensitive data, tailored to the organization’s needs. These layers offer a starting point for building a self-managed payment environment with controls across the stack.

The takeaway is straightforward: MongoDB Enterprise Advanced, MCK, and OpenShift can provide a practical foundation for running a payment application on infrastructure the same organization controls.

title: Atlas for Government: The Only FedRAMP® Class D Certified Cross-Cloud Operational Database
summary:
Federal, state, and local agencies are under mounting pressure to modernize legacy systems, adopt AI, and protect sensitive data, all at the same time. Many of the databases that can currently handle an agency's most sensitive, high-impact workloads are native to a single cloud and run nowhere else, leaving agencies with a limited set of authorized options and little room to change course when missions, mandates, or threats shift.

MongoDB is the intelligent data platform for the AI era, and today we're extending it to the workloads where the stakes are highest: MongoDB Atlas for Government has achieved FedRAMP® Class D Certification. Formerly known as FedRAMP High, Class D is the highest level of assessment under the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP). Atlas for Government has also added support for Azure Government, expanding its existing support for AWS GovCloud and Commercial Regions and Google Cloud Assured Workloads.

Together, these milestones make MongoDB Atlas for Government the only FedRAMP Class D (High) Certified cross-cloud operational database in the world. Public sector organizations and the independent software vendors (ISVs) that serve them can now run their most sensitive mission-critical workloads—including production AI applications built on real-time operational data—on a single platform and on the cloud provider of their choice, across AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud. To learn more, visit the MongoDB Atlas for Government product page or the FedRAMP Marketplace page.

What is MongoDB Atlas for Government?

MongoDB Atlas for Government is an independent, dedicated environment of the MongoDB Atlas intelligent data platform built specifically for the U.S. public sector and the ISVs that build government solutions. It brings the core capabilities of MongoDB’s intelligent data platform to government, giving agencies a fully managed way to deploy, run, and scale mission-critical applications in the cloud, including transactional workloads, search, vector search for AI applications, and time series data, all within a single, unified data platform.

Atlas for Government is operated by MongoDB employees who are United States persons on U.S. soil, and all encryption within MongoDB-managed infrastructure is FIPS 140-3 validated. The platform maintains a 99.995% uptime SLA and has been generally available since 2021.

MongoDB Atlas for Government is already trusted across the federal government. MongoDB works with 13 U.S. Federal Cabinet-level agencies. With FedRAMP Class D (High) certification, agencies like these can bring even more sensitive, high-impact workloads to Atlas for Government. For example, a health agency could modernize benefits and eligibility systems that handle protected health information and personally identifiable information. A financial agency could run real-time fraud detection across high-volume transaction streams. And a civilian agency could build an AI application that lets analysts search policy and case records in natural language, without that data leaving a FedRAMP Class D (High) environment.

What is FedRAMP Class D (High)?

FedRAMP provides the standardized authorization framework that cloud service providers (CSPs) must successfully navigate to demonstrate compliance with federal security requirements before hosting federal agency workloads. In 2026, FedRAMP moved away from labeling these standards Low, Moderate, and High, replacing them with a four-tier Certification Class system, A through D. FedRAMP Class D (High) is the direct successor to what was previously known as FedRAMP High, and it remains the most rigorous tier a CSP can achieve within the FedRAMP program.

FedRAMP Class D (High) certification is designed for cloud services that support an agency's high-impact systems, where a security failure could have severe or catastrophic consequences for operations, assets, or people. This includes systems tied to national security, law enforcement, and emergency response, as well as high-impact modernization initiatives across civilian agencies. Achieving this certification requires meeting hundreds of stringent security controls covering everything from access management to incident response.

MongoDB Atlas for Government achieved FedRAMP Moderate authorization in 2023 and has been a trusted, fully managed data platform for federal agencies and ISVs since then. With FedRAMP Class D (High) certification, that foundation is now extended to high-impact workloads, including production AI applications. Agencies can bring those workloads to the cloud on a platform that meets the security and compliance requirements for high-impact systems, and build secure, production-grade AI applications on top of them.

Freedom to run anywhere: Now spanning AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud

With the addition of support for Azure Government, MongoDB Atlas for Government now runs across all three major cloud providers: AWS (both GovCloud and AWS commercial regions), Google Cloud (via Assured Workloads), and Azure Government. This makes MongoDB Atlas for Government the only FedRAMP Class D (High) certified, cross-cloud database in the world.

For public sector organizations, this cross-cloud support is about more than convenience. A database tied to a single cloud provider limits an agency's options if costs rise, a mission requirement changes, or a new mandate calls for a different cloud environment. MongoDB Atlas for Government gives agencies and ISVs the freedom to run their workloads on the cloud that best fits their needs today, and to change that decision later without rewriting their applications. Within FedRAMP-certified cloud environments (AWS GovCloud, Google Cloud Assured Workloads, and Azure Government), data can be distributed across providers to optimize for performance, cost, or resilience, and to strengthen disaster recovery with automatic failover across providers.

Getting started on Azure Government works the same way as it does on AWS GovCloud or Google Cloud Assured Workloads. Agencies and ISVs can create a project in Atlas for Government, designate it as a FedRAMP Class D (High) Gov Regions Only project, and select Azure as the cloud provider when creating a cluster.

Protecting data and powering AI at the highest level

FedRAMP Class D (High) sets a high bar for how a provider documents, assesses, and maintains its security program, but that is only one part of the picture. Agencies handling the country's most sensitive data also need assurance that the data itself stays protected, even if a system is compromised.

MongoDB Atlas for Government provides robust protection for sensitive data, supporting workloads that include Personally Identifiable Information (PII), Protected Health Information (PHI), and Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) data. Data at rest is protected using database encryption with Customer Managed Keys, and data in transit is protected via TLS.

For organizations that require protection beyond the authorization boundary, MongoDB Queryable Encryption performs encryption and decryption client-side, so designated fields remain encrypted throughout their lifecycle, in transit, at rest, and in use. MongoDB, cloud operators, and even the organization's own database administrators never have access to keys or unencrypted data.

This same secure foundation enables agencies to deploy production AI applications in their high-impact environments. MongoDB Atlas for Government includes MongoDB Vector Search, allowing teams to build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and other AI-powered applications directly on top of their operational data. Instead of standing up a separate vector database and building a pipeline to keep it in sync, agencies can run transactional workloads, search, and vector search in a single, FedRAMP Class D-certified environment, reducing both complexity and risk.

How to get started with MongoDB Atlas for Government

With FedRAMP Class D (High) certification and support for Azure Government, MongoDB’s intelligent data platform for the AI era now reaches the public sector’s highest-stakes missions. MongoDB Atlas for Government gives public sector organizations and ISVs a secure, fully managed, and truly multi-cloud way to run their most sensitive workloads and build production AI applications.

To get started, visit the MongoDB Atlas for Government product page, view the FedRAMP Marketplace listing, or refer to the Atlas for Government documentation for setup details.

FAQ

What is MongoDB Atlas for Government?

MongoDB Atlas for Government is an independent, dedicated environment of MongoDB Atlas built for the U.S. public sector and the ISVs that build government solutions. It is a fully managed, FedRAMP Class D (High) certified operational database.

What is FedRAMP Class D (High)?

FedRAMP Class D (High) is the highest tier in FedRAMP’s four-tier Certification Class system and the direct successor to what was previously known as FedRAMP High. It is designed for cloud services that support high-impact government systems.

Which cloud providers does Atlas for Government support?

Atlas for Government runs on AWS (GovCloud and Commercial Regions), Google Cloud (via Assured Workloads), and Azure Government. Within FedRAMP-certified cloud environments, data can be distributed across providers with automatic failover.

Can agencies build AI applications on Atlas for Government?

Yes. MongoDB Vector Search enables teams to build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and other AI applications directly on operational data, in a single FedRAMP Class D (High) certified environment, without a separate vector database or sync pipeline.

title: Diagnosing MongoDB Search Performance with Atlas Metrics
summary:
Your MongoDB Atlas metrics show elevated disk I/O, high search CPU, increasing query latency, or a rising search max replication lag. Like when your car’s mysterious “check engine” light comes on, these signals can mean different things. To figure out the issue, you’ll want to start by identifying which process and metric is under pressure.

Scaling the database tier may provide temporary relief, but it does not separate the search and operational workloads. When mongot and mongod share nodes, search can compete with database activity for memory, disk I/O, and CPU. The right response depends on whether the index does not fit in available memory, the workloads contend during traffic spikes, or possibly even both occurring simultaneously.

This post explains how to diagnose slow search performance, decide whether dedicated search nodes are the right fix, and size them correctly if they are.

Why tackling the underlying issue matters

The default response to slow search is often to scale up the database tier. More RAM and CPU can help the database portion of the workload, but they do not create a separate resource budget for search on a co-located deployment.

Two cases can produce similar symptoms, but they call for different responses. With index-size pressure, the Search index is larger than the memory available to mongot, so queries page data from disk even when database activity is low. A larger Search tier with enough memory addresses this problem; isolation by itself does not. With resource contention, the index fits in memory, but search latency rises when database reads, writes, or replication become busy. Separate search nodes address this contention by giving mongot different CPU, memory, and disk resources.

The distinction matters when you select a tier. Dedicated search nodes remove competition with database workloads, but they still need to be sized correctly.

Search nodes explained

MongoDB Search and MongoDB Vector Search use mongot, the search process that maintains and queries search indexes. mongod is the database process that stores application data and handles database operations. In a colocated deployment, both processes run on the same nodes.

Dedicated search nodes run mongot on separate infrastructure from the nodes running mongod. Dedicated search nodes provide workload isolation for search, similar to how Analytics Nodes isolate analytical workloads.

With dedicated search nodes, database nodes handle operational reads and writes while search nodes handle search queries and index work. Each workload gets its own memory budget, CPU capacity, and scaling lifecycle. This applies to both MongoDB Search and MongoDB Vector Search on Atlas.

Why colocated search runs into resource constraints

When mongot and mongod share nodes, memory and CPU are common sources of resource pressure. WiredTiger, the operating system, and mongot share RAM; if the index is larger than the memory available to mongot, queries may read index pages from disk. Search queries and background indexing also compete with database reads, writes, and replication for CPU time, so latency can rise even when the index fits in memory.

Atlas metrics help show which process is under pressure and whether the issue is paging or contention. Look at these signals together rather than treating any one metric as a diagnosis:

  • Search Page Fault, which reports average page faults per second in the Search process

  • Search Process Memory and Search Index Size compared with the node's RAM

  • Search Normalized Process CPU compared with Normalized System CPU

  • Search Process Throttling, which indicates that work is arriving faster than the Search process can admit it

  • Search query latency and Search Max Replication Lag

If database CPU and memory look healthy while Search metrics are under pressure, Search is consuming the resources available to it. That does not identify the root cause by itself. Compare index size with available memory to test for paging; compare latency and Search CPU with database activity to test for contention.

If page faults and latency stay high while the database is quiet, Search needs more memory. If latency only rises when the database gets busy, the two workloads are competing.

How dedicated search nodes separate search and database workloads

Memory isolation and cache performance

On a colocated node, the memory shown in the Atlas tier specification is shared. WiredTiger uses part of it for the database cache, the operating system and runtime need additional memory, and the remainder is available to mongot. The exact amount varies with tier and workload, and there is no fixed co-located cache size for mongot.

Dedicated search nodes give mongot a separate memory budget. MongoDB documentation describes approximately 90% of search node RAM as available for index data, with the remainder used by the JVM and other process needs. MongoDB Search indexes do not need to fit entirely in memory. A single query usually touches only part of the index, and the OS keeps the frequently used pages in RAM. MongoDB Vector Search is different and works best when the index fits in memory.

When there is sufficient memory to accommodate the majority of the index data, sustained page faults should reduce and latency should become more stable. If page faults remain high after migration to search nodes, the Search tier may still be undersized, or the workload may have another bottleneck. Isolation will help, but if this is an index sizing issue at the core, you may need to combine this approach with other techniques. Those techniques could include switching from dynamic mapping to static mapping on specific fields, using alternate tokenization strategies other than nGram for autocomplete fields, leveraging vector quantization for vector search indexes, and other actions needed to reduce the size of the index.

CPU separation and parallel segment search

Search queries and index updates can consume substantial CPU. Separate search nodes prevent database traffic from taking those cores during the same interval. For $search queries, parallel segment search can search multiple Lucene segments concurrently when enabled with the query's concurrent option. For $vectorSearch queries, concurrent segment search is on by default on search nodes. The Search tier's CPU count limits the parallelism available.

MongoDB Search might fall back to single-threaded execution when too many concurrent queries are queued. Treat parallel segment search as additional capacity, not as a guarantee that every query will run in parallel. Monitor query latency, Search Normalized Process CPU, and Search Process Throttling under representative concurrency.

No competition with operational traffic

Search Max Replication Lag means index staleness: How far behind mongot is in applying changes from the mongod oplog to a MongoDB Search or MongoDB Vector Search index. This is different from replica set replication lag, which measures how far secondary mongod members are behind the primary.

Isolation removes one cause of Search Max Replication Lag: Indexing work from mongot competing with mongod for CPU on the same node. It does not remove the indexing work. mongot still reads every change from mongod and applies it to the search index on search nodes.

Isolation does not resolve issues due to write-heavy workloads. Sustained write volumes and the amount of indexing work created by each change can increase index staleness. Factors include the number of indexed fields, autocomplete fields using nGram or edgeGram tokenizers, and embeddedDocuments mappings where one document change can rewrite many Lucene documents. Indexes get updated when their associated documents and fields change; minimally, one write to a document will generate at least one corresponding write to the index(es) (where the indexed field is updated). Schema changes or sharding may be required with dedicated nodes to optimally support the workload.

Replica set replication lag is separate. Search nodes may reduce CPU contention that affects the database, but they do not guarantee lower replica set lag or lower Search Max Replication Lag when write or indexing volume remains high.

Example: From page faults to consistent search performance

Consider a co-located M30 deployment with 8 GB of RAM per node. As an illustration rather than a fixed Atlas allocation, about 2 GB may go to the WiredTiger cache and at least 1 GB to the OS, mongod, connections, and other runtime needs, leaving about 5 GB or less for mongot. If the Search index is 6 GB, sustained Search Page Fault activity is highly likely. The database may show low CPU and healthy memory metrics while Search still reads index data from disk.

Before search nodes

In this example, the co-located deployment is an M30 with 8 GB RAM per node and a 6 GB Search index. Atlas metrics show sustained non-zero Search Page Fault during normal traffic, and search query latency p95 is 650 ms. Validate the estimated 5 GB or less available to mongot against the actual metrics.

After search nodes

Assume the workload moves to an S40 Search tier with 16 GB of RAM per node. Using the documented approximate 90% allocation as a planning estimate gives about 14.4 GB for index data, leaving room for a 6 GB index and query working set. Validate the tier's available memory and observed behavior in Atlas rather than treating the estimate as a guarantee.

After the move, the dedicated S40 Search tier has about 14.4 GB of memory available for the same 6 GB index. In this example, Search Page Fault falls after the index is resident, except during warm-up or workload changes, and search query latency p95 is 120 ms.

Performance improves once Atlas finishes building the index on the search nodes and routes queries to them. During the build, queries continue to use the existing colocated indexes, and index construction adds read load to the database cluster. Plan for that transition instead of expecting a change when the Search Nodes are first deployed.

When to move to dedicated search nodes

Dedicated search nodes are not necessary for every slow query: if an index fits comfortably in available memory and latency targets are met without contention, co-location may remain the simpler choice. The example above shows why a team might move when paging indicates that the Search index does not fit the memory budget. In production, look for a pattern across several signals before choosing a dedicated tier:

  • Sustained non-zero Search Page Fault with an index that approaches or exceeds available Search memory

  • Search Process Throttling remaining above zero, indicating that work is arriving faster than the Search process can admit it

  • High Search Normalized Process CPU or a high Search-to-system CPU ratio during query traffic

  • Search latency that rises when database activity increases

  • Search Max Replication Lag that rises with indexing activity, after ruling out write volume and index-mapping causes

  • Query latency targets that require consistent performance

  • Repeated database scaling to accommodate Search growth

On a colocated node, total disk I/O combines mongod and mongot activity, so disk IOPS alone is a weak signal for Search diagnosis. Start with Search Page Fault to attribute paging to the Search process, and use total disk IOPS as corroborating evidence.

Best practices

These checks make a tier decision more reliable: they help identify whether the bottleneck is memory, CPU, or indexing work, and when to plan the migration. Use the relevant metrics together, and account for the workload and operational requirements before changing deployment architecture.

  • Check Search Process Memory, Search Index Size, and Search Page Fault together when testing for memory pressure.

  • Check Search Normalized Process CPU, Normalized System CPU, latency, and Search Process Throttling together when testing for contention or saturation.

  • Treat Search Max Replication Lag as index staleness, and investigate replica set replication lag separately.

  • Size Search Nodes for both index memory and query or indexing CPU; plan for index growth and concurrency.

  • Confirm prerequisites before migration. Dedicated search nodes require an M10 or higher cluster, so upgrade a Flex cluster before attempting to use them.

  • Expect an index-building period before query routing changes, then monitor the search nodes after the cutover.

What workload isolation enables

Analytics nodes separate analytical workloads from operational database traffic. Dedicated search nodes apply the same workload-isolation model to MongoDB Search and MongoDB Vector Search, allowing each infrastructure tier to be sized for its own workload.

The result is easier diagnosis and more predictable behavior. Page faults can be addressed with sufficient Search memory, CPU contention can be addressed with isolation, and indexing lag can be investigated using write volume and index-mapping details rather than treated as a generic replication problem. Views for search indexes, quantization for vector indexes, sharding, and other techniques can also be used with isolation to further improve performance. Search index partitioning can also extend the capacity of supported deployments beyond a single index or node's limits; consult the current MongoDB documentation for those limits.

Next steps

Use the metrics to identify whether memory pressure, workload contention, or indexing volume is limiting performance. Then use the deployment guidance to assess the appropriate Search tier and plan a migration if dedicated nodes fit the diagnosis.

  • Review MongoDB Search metrics for Search Process Memory, Search Index Size, Search Page Fault, and Search Process Throttling.

  • Identify whether page faults indicate an index-memory problem or whether latency follows database activity and indicates contention.

  • Check Search Max Replication Lag and replica set replication lag as separate metrics with separate investigations.

  • Review tips for sizing and scaling Search Nodes and MongoDB Vector Search production sizing.

  • Account for index build time and the temporary read load before evaluating post-migration performance.

title: Bring Live MongoDB Atlas Data Into Microsoft 365 Copilot
summary:
The federated Copilot connector for MongoDB Atlas gives organizations a governed way to bring live operational data into the flow of work across Copilot experiences.

To operate efficiently, businesses require timely information about the systems that underpin their organizations. For example, they need to be able to answer questions like: Which incidents are open? Which orders are delayed? What fields and data types are present in the customer collection? The answers they need often live in operational applications built on MongoDB Atlas, while the questions are asked in the productivity tools people use every day.

To help close that gap, MongoDB is excited to introduce a federated Copilot connector for MongoDB Atlas. Now generally available, the connector enables users to ask Microsoft 365 Copilot questions about live data in MongoDB Atlas, bringing operational context into the same experience where people collaborate, analyze information, and make decisions.

The connector surfaces MongoDB Atlas data across Microsoft Copilot experiences, including Copilot Chat, Researcher in Copilot, Copilot Cowork, Microsoft Word, Excel, and Teams, with additional experiences planned to follow.

Bring operational data into the flow of work

The connector brings MongoDB Atlas to Microsoft Copilot through MongoDB’s managed remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. When a user asks a relevant question, Copilot can query Atlas in real time—instead of relying on a static copy of the data.

This creates a more direct path from a business question to the information needed to answer it, and helps users—who may not have MongoDB expertise—access and analyze live operational data through an AI assistant.

Now, business users can use conversational prompts to:

  • Retrieve live business data without writing database queries.

  • Find and filter customers, transactions, products, orders, content, or operational events.

  • Get quick counts and key performance indicators, such as the number of delayed orders or high-value customers.

  • Summarize and rank data to identify top categories, products, regions, trends, averages, and other business insights.

title: Build Once, Grow Freely: Search and Vector Search on Atlas Infinite
summary:
Enterprise workloads are getting bigger, more variable, and harder to predict, especially as agentic applications introduce spiky, unpredictable demand. Most data platforms weren't built for this reality—to cope with demand, they bolt AI services onto aging architecture, leaving customers to manage, monitor, and pay for multiple systems to get the job done. That fragmentation slows your teams down and limits how fast and how far your agentic applications can run.

In a traditional database architecture, storage is tied to the machine that runs your queries. Scaling up, adding a replica, or restoring a backup comes down to copying data from one machine to another, and the bigger the database, the longer that takes. My colleague Abhishek Chauhan calls this “storage gravity.” “Data doesn’t want to move,” he wrote for the MongoDB Engineering Blog. The bigger the data gets, the harder it pulls.

MongoDB built Atlas Infinite precisely for this reality; purpose-built to absorb spikes in demand with flexible, elastic scaling. Whether you’re launching a first prototype or running at petabyte-scale in production, Atlas Infinite enables you to build on a foundation that scales with you and never forces re-architecture. With MongoDB Search and Vector Search supported on Atlas Infinite in public preview, your database and retrieval live in one platform, with nothing to stitch together.

How Atlas Infinite works

A new deployment option within MongoDB Atlas, Atlas Infinite separates compute from storage so each scales independently and rapidly. Storage moves into a fully managed layer that handles replication, durability, and backup across availability zones, so compute no longer has to carry the data with it.

The impact is dramatic. Read replicas come online in minutes because there's no data to copy. A single shard holds up to 128 TB, so you no longer shard just to add disk space. You only pay for the data you store, not capacity provisioned in advance, so a small team never has to buy a bigger compute tier just to get more disk. And it’s all driven by the same MongoDB API, drivers, and tooling, so your application doesn’t need to change.

The separation of storage and compute matters most where agentic applications grow fastest: the retrieval layer. Every answer an assistant gives and every step an agent takes starts with a search over your data, and the data behind that search, especially vector embeddings, can grow large quickly. With MongoDB Search and Vector Search running natively on Atlas Infinite, that data lives on the same foundation as the rest of your application and can grow without re-architecture. Build your agentic workload once and keep scaling it on the same foundation as demand grows.

Figure 1. Compute and storage as independent layers in Atlas Infinite.

Retrieval, built into the database

Many retrieval stacks are cobbled together from disconnected components—a database, a search engine, and a vector database—which means running all of those separate parts, plus managing the pipelines that keep everything in sync. On Atlas Infinite, retrieval is part of the platform, so there are fewer pieces to build, secure, and maintain. Here is what that looks like:

  • One platform, nothing to stitch together: On Atlas Infinite, your database and retrieval work together seamlessly, with no separate search engine or vector database to stand up, sync, or monitor. MongoDB Atlas keeps your indexes in sync with your data automatically, so there is no pipeline for your team to build or maintain, and no extra systems to copy sensitive data into or secure. With Atlas Infinite, retrieval is built in, alongside the ability to scale to absorb unpredictable demand with zero waste.
  • Start small, never outgrow your data platform: A team can start with a 5 GB prototype that includes semantic search and keep building on the same foundation. Rather than sizing and maintaining two infrastructures, storage grows automatically with your data, billed only for what you store. The operational data behind your search has room to grow to petabyte scale on Atlas Infinite, with no re-platforming when the application takes off.
  • Agent memory and context retrieval: Give agents one place to store and retrieve context, history, and state alongside your operational data. Support thousands of agents hitting your retrieval layer while also persisting agent memory and context within a single, durable system that scales when they need it.

Figure 2. Search and Vector Search run alongside the database on Atlas Infinite, with indexes kept in sync automatically and data stored once in Atlas-managed storage.

How Atlas Infinite handles your largest text and vector workloads

Separating compute from storage in the database also changes the scaling behavior and economics of large retrieval workloads. Text and vector data lives in the database first, where it drives storage requirements. Because Atlas Infinite manages that storage separately from compute, the economics come down to one property of the data: how well it compresses.

Databases shrink data on disk with compression, which works by finding repetition. Text is full of repetition: common words, repeated field names, predictable structure. Text in MongoDB typically compresses to about 40% of its original size. An embedding is an array of decimal values with almost no repetition, so it shrinks by only about 13%. In practice, a vector takes up as much space on disk as it does in your application.

How each deployment option stores that data

Atlas Core uses attached storage volumes. Each node in a replica set keeps a full copy of the data on its own disk, provisioned ahead of time with room to grow, and compute and storage come in matched tiers. That gives every node complete isolation and predictable performance, and it's the right fit for many workloads, especially ones where data and query load grow together.

Vector workloads tend to be storage-driven because high-dimension embeddings are so large. A RAG knowledge base can hold hundreds of gigabytes of embeddings, which drives up storage needs relative to query volume. On Atlas Core, storage can drive scaling decisions: once you outgrow a tier’s maximum disk size, you have to move up a tier to get more storage, even if you don’t need more compute, and very large datasets eventually call for sharding.

On Atlas Infinite, compute and storage scale independently. Storage is billed per logical (uncompressed) GB of data you store, metered hourly. Replication across availability zones happens inside the storage layer and isn't billed separately. There's no headroom to provision, and because a shard holds up to 128 TB, a growing dataset doesn't push you to a larger compute tier or to more shards. Because embeddings barely compress, their logical size and their size on disk are nearly the same, so you pay only for the data you store and nothing for the copies and headroom underneath it. As vector collections grow to hundreds of millions of documents, that billing model becomes an advantage.

Here is an example. For a collection with 100 million documents, each with a 1,024-dimension float32 embedding and about 1 KB of other fields, storage is roughly 500 GB uncompressed. Assuming moderate query traffic, an M30 cluster tier’s compute is sufficient.

On Atlas Core, since embeddings barely compress, the data shrinks to ~435 GB on disk. Each node also needs space for the oplog and room for the collection to grow. At 1.3× headroom, that comes to about 565 GB per node, more than the 512 GB an M30 supports, so the cluster has to move up to an M40 for the disk. On Atlas Infinite, the cluster stays at the compute tier its queries need, and storage is billed once on the 500 GB it holds. With storage billed once and no tier-up for disk, the total monthly cost of this deployment, Search Nodes included, comes out about 25% lower than on Core. At 1 billion vectors (about 5 TB), it is about 30% lower, and the gap keeps widening as vector data grows. These figures are modeled on list prices in US East, with Search Nodes sized to the smallest tier that fits the index, so your results will vary.

Where the difference is smaller

Text-heavy search workloads also see a TCO benefit on Atlas Infinite, around 5% to 10% cost reduction at multi-terabyte scale. Text compresses well, so Core's storage cost per GB is already low. The advantage of Atlas Infinite comes from deferring early tier-ups and delaying sharding for disk. Under 500 GB, the two deployment options are roughly even on cost, so a smaller workload gets Atlas Infinite’s room to grow without paying more for it. Choose the deployment option based on the elasticity and growth you expect.

Get started with Search and Vector Search on Atlas Infinite

MongoDB Search and Vector Search are available on Atlas Infinite in public preview on AWS. Choose Atlas Infinite as the deployment option for your next workload, add a search index the way you would on Atlas Core, and keep building on the same foundation as your application grows. Whether you’re prototyping an AI feature or running a large production application, you can start small and keep going. Start with the Atlas Infinite documentation.

title: Persistent Sessions and Memory for Strands with MongoDB
summary:
Today, we’re launching the MongoDB Strands Harness SDK Integration, available now as the open-source strands-mongodb Python package. Strands, built and maintained by AWS, is an open-source framework for building AI agents. With this integration, MongoDB becomes the single data platform behind your Strands agents, providing:

  • Session persistence, so agents can resume conversations and complex tasks after a restart or on a different instance.

  • Long-term memory for facts and lessons that carry across conversations.

  • Vector search to retrieve relevant past interactions by meaning.

Strands’ MemoryManager decides what to remember and when to recall it, while MongoDB handles where it’s stored and how it’s retrieved, so there’s no custom memory code to build or maintain. And because your operational data already lives in MongoDB, agents can use Atlas Vector Search to ground their answers in it, with no copy synced to a separate vector database.

What is the Strands Harness SDK?

The Strands Harness SDK helps developers build AI agents. It manages the agent loop while giving developers control over how agents execute tasks and maintain context. Support for memory, sessions, and hooks lets developers shape agent behavior and connect agents to their application’s data and persistence layer. It provides pluggable storage and memory interfaces, with built-in backends for local files and Amazon S3. Integrations like this one let you swap in another backing service without rewriting your agent’s core logic.

Why do sessions need a database?

Say a team deploys its Strands agent as an AWS Lambda function, callable as an internal service by teams across the company. Every invocation runs in a disposable environment (i.e., a scratchpad for the agent). There may be no local disk, and no guarantee that the next invocation lands on the same instance, so the state tied to one process is invisible to the next.

With this integration, every agent session is saved in MongoDB. Each invocation loads the session by its ID and carries on, regardless of which instance handled the last turn. Long-term memories the agent saves to MongoDBMemoryStore persist beyond the session, so they’re available the next time that user returns.

Figure 1. Stateless agent architecture keeps state out of the agent process.

Two Lambda instances serve consecutive turns of the same session. Both read and write the session via MongoDBStorage and long-term memory via MongoDBMemoryStore, so neither depends on the other's local state. That matters most for enterprises with many teams running Strands agents across different machines. They get one MongoDB-backed foundation for agent state and memory, instead of building and maintaining separate systems to store and retrieve sessions and memory.

What does the MongoDB Strands Harness SDK Integration provide?

This integration covers three core areas:

  • Cross-environment continuity: When a different instance handles the next request, or a user returns after a restart, the agent retrieves its saved session from MongoDB. Continuity doesn't depend on any machine.

  • Resilience to failure: If a host crashes or a container is rescheduled, another instance resumes the session from the last turn written to MongoDB.

  • Retention and control: You decide how long sessions and memories are retained, with separate retention periods for each. A memory store can also delete a single memory, or all of its memories, on demand. Everything lives alongside your application's operational data in MongoDB, under the access controls and backups you already have in place.

The memory store also handles what production agents run into:

  • No duplicate memories: Strands can extract the same fact more than once. A content hash turns the repeat into a no-op. For example, if the agent extracts "Prefers metric units and a 24-hour clock" a second time, the store keeps the copy it already has, with its original timestamp and expiry. This means that, as a developer, you don’t need to write your own deduplication logic, and your memory store stays clean, regardless of how often the agent re-extracts the same fact.

  • Tenant scope: The store stamps every memory with a scope, such as a tenant or user ID, and limits every search and delete to that scope. Callers can't override it through filters or metadata. This isolation is enforced by the package, not by the server, so where a tenant boundary is also a compliance boundary, give each tenant its own database or collection, with credentials restricted to it, and MongoDB enforces the boundary itself.

  • Search adapts to your deployment: The integration supports Vector Search, Text Search via Atlas Search, or Hybrid Search combined with $rankFusion. The store automatically selects the optimal method available in your deployment, and each result indicates which search type was used.

  • OpenTelemetry tracing. Every operation records a span on the tracer your application already uses, and no memory content is captured.

How it works

Memory, with no embedding pipeline to run: Atlas Automated Embedding embeds each memory for you, using voyage-4-lite unless you choose a different model. You write plain text and search with plain text. There's no embedding library to install and no model API key to manage. Atlas generates, stores, and updates the embeddings itself as memories are written, so there's no batch job to keep vectors in step with the text.

As you can see above, the query and the stored fact share no words, but the store still finds it. This path needs an Atlas cluster with an embedding model registered. If you already produce your own embeddings, the store can index and query them instead; the README covers the additional code required.

Figure 2. Without an embedding pipeline, memory is just text in and text out. Atlas generates and stores the embeddings and embeds each query before running $vectorSearch.

store.add() writes plain text and returns. Atlas embeds it in the background, and embeds each search query the same way before running $vectorSearch. Bringing your own embedding model is optional.

Sessions and memory together: One connection config serves both. Hand them to the agent and let the SDK wire them up:

The storage= parameter makes MongoDB the default backend for five SDK subsystems, including sessions, context offloading, and transcripts. The SDK's SnapshotSessionManager saves the conversation under its session ID, and any agent built with that ID restores it. MemoryManager gives the model a tool to search memory and, with add_tool_config=True, one to save to it. There's no MongoDB-specific session class to learn.

Figure 3. After a Strands agent is wired to MongoDB, it can save and restore conversations and search long-term memory without any MongoDB-specific session code.

Three agent parameters do the wiring. storage= points the SDK's storage subsystems at MongoDBStorage, session_manager= saves and restores the conversation by session ID, and memory_manager= gives the model search and save tools backed by MongoDBMemoryStore.

Explore the source, open issues, or contribute on GitHub. 

The README covers connection options, the full configuration reference, and index privileges.

There may be no local disk, and no guarantee that the next invocation lands on the same instance, so the state tied to one process is invisible to the next.

With this integration, every agent session is saved in MongoDB. Each invocation loads the session by its ID and carries on, regardless of which instance handled the last turn. Long-term memories the agent saves to MongoDBMemoryStore persist beyond the session, so they’re available the next time that user returns.

Figure 1. Stateless agent architecture keeps state out of the agent process.

Two Lambda instances serve consecutive turns of the same session. Both read and write the session via MongoDBStorage and long-term memory via MongoDBMemoryStore, so neither depends on the other's local state. That matters most for enterprises with many teams running Strands agents across different machines. They get one MongoDB-backed foundation for agent state and memory, instead of building and maintaining separate systems to store and retrieve sessions and memory.

What does the MongoDB Strands Harness SDK Integration provide?

This integration covers three core areas:

  • Cross-environment continuity: When a different instance handles the next request, or a user returns after a restart, the agent retrieves its saved session from MongoDB. Continuity doesn't depend on any machine.

  • Resilience to failure: If a host crashes or a container is rescheduled, another instance resumes the session from the last turn written to MongoDB.

  • Retention and control: You decide how long sessions and memories are retained, with separate retention periods for each. A memory store can also delete a single memory, or all of its memories, on demand. Everything lives alongside your application's operational data in MongoDB, under the access controls and backups you already have in place.

The memory store also handles what production agents run into:

  • No duplicate memories: Strands can extract the same fact more than once. A content hash turns the repeat into a no-op. For example, if the agent extracts "Prefers metric units and a 24-hour clock" a second time, the store keeps the copy it already has, with its original timestamp and expiry.   • Tenant scope: The store stamps every memory with a scope, such as a tenant or user ID, and limits every search and delete to that scope. Callers can't override it through filters or metadata.   • Search adapts to your deployment: The integration supports Vector Search, Text Search via Atlas Search, or Hybrid Search combined with $rankFusion. The store automatically selects the optimal method available in your deployment, and each result indicates which search type was used.

  • OpenTelemetry tracing. Every operation records a span on the tracer your application already uses, and no memory content is captured.

Memory, with no embedding pipeline to run: Atlas Automated Embedding embeds each memory for you, using voyage-4-lite unless you choose a different model. You write plain text and search with plain text. There's no embedding library to install and no model API key to manage. Atlas generates, stores, and updates the embeddings itself as memories are written, so there's no batch job to keep vectors in step with the text.

As you can see above, the query and the stored fact share no words, but the store still finds it. This path needs an Atlas cluster with an embedding model registered. If you already produce your own embeddings, the store can index and query them instead; the README covers the additional code required.

Figure 2. Without an embedding pipeline, memory is just text in and text out. Atlas generates and stores the embeddings and embeds each query before running $vectorSearch.

store.add() writes plain text and returns. Atlas embeds it in the background, and embeds each search query the same way before running $vectorSearch. Bringing your own embedding model is optional.

Sessions and memory together: One connection config serves both. Hand them to the agent and let the SDK wire them up:

The storage= parameter makes MongoDB the default backend for five SDK subsystems, including sessions, context offloading, and transcripts. The SDK's SnapshotSessionManager saves the conversation under its session ID, and any agent built with that ID restores it. MemoryManager gives the model a tool to search memory and, with add_tool_config=True, one to save to it. There's no MongoDB-specific session class to learn.

Figure 3. After a Strands agent is wired to MongoDB, it can save and restore conversations and search long-term memory without any MongoDB-specific session code.

Three agent parameters do the wiring. storage= points the SDK's storage subsystems at MongoDBStorage, session_manager= saves and restores the conversation by session ID, and memory_manager= gives the model search and save tools backed by MongoDBMemoryStore.

title: MongoDB Named a Leader in Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Cloud Operational Database Management Systems 2026
summary:
I’m thrilled to share that MongoDB has been named a Leader in the new Gartner Magic Quadrant for Cloud Operational Database Management Systems.

We believe our placement as a Leader in a brand-new category reflects the investments MongoDB has made in our data platform and the strength of our product offerings. We also believe it reflects the trust our more than 70,000 customers, including ~75% of the Fortune 100, have placed in MongoDB.

Agents are changing what an operational database has to do: absorb spiky demand, keep context fresh, and keep cost per task down. Here’s how we see MongoDB doing that, and what it means for your next architecture decision.

What is the operational database category?

This year, the former Gartner Magic Quadrant for Cloud Database Management Systems has been split into separate Magic Quadrant reports for Operational Database and Lakehouse, because we believe the buying criteria and decision-makers associated with each differ. If you’re choosing the database that runs your apps and agents, you now have a report written for that decision.

Gartner defines the market for cloud operational database management systems (DBMS) as software designed to store and manipulate data and delivered primarily as platform as a service (PaaS) in the cloud. These systems primarily optimize routine business transactions, data writes, and application state management. They prioritize high concurrency and low latency while enforcing transactional guarantees to ensure data integrity.¹

Put plainly, these systems power the services that the world depends on, from healthcare and telecommunications to card payments and banking, to retail solutions that touch millions of people.

Why your data platform is important to AI success

I traveled a lot in 2026, meeting with scores of MongoDB customers and partners across dozens of cities (in multiple countries!). One theme kept coming up: the data platform decides whether AI works. A few threads connect what I’ve been hearing:

  • Agents make demand spikier. Where a person might click a button or two to accomplish a task, an agent will make dozens of calls (and might even spawn other agents). That's why elasticity matters more than another point of peak throughput.

  • Cost per task, not cost per token or cost per seat, is what organizations looking to control AI spending should focus on. As my colleague Pete Johnson has written, the goal of every org should be spending the right 200K tokens instead of the wrong million. When your operational data, vector search, and reranking live in the same platform, you can filter, retrieve, and rerank in one pipeline—saving money and improving results.

  • One data foundation is simpler to run. Teams build AI applications directly on MongoDB’s intelligent data platform instead of governing separate components. As Jacky Koh, Co-founder of Relevance AI, put it, “Having both the operational and vector database in the same platform makes managing scale much simpler and managing performance much more effective.”

In our opinion, AI success depends on having the right data platform. MongoDB combines a state-of-the-art operational database with search, vector search, hybrid search, and built-in embedding models that keep context fresh (giving agents the information they need to act reliably). MongoDB also gives customers the freedom to run anywhere, helping them move quickly today while enabling them to change deployment postures later.

How MongoDB enables (AI) innovation

2026 was another big year for MongoDB. Everything we do aims to help organizations move faster, build smarter, and to simplify complex architectures, and 2026 was no different.

The product releases and capabilities we shared this year reinforce the importance of data to AI success, and underscore how MongoDB is the intelligent data platform for the AI era. Here are some highlights:

  • MongoDB 9.0 

    • 9.0 is the fastest, most performant version of MongoDB we’ve ever built, and it’s designed for applications and agents that act on live data. Compared to MongoDB 8.0, transactional workloads in 9.0 achieve up to 20% higher throughput, enabling applications to process more business-critical operations more efficiently. Find-one queries are up to 35% faster, and update-one queries are up to 30% faster. That means more users, transactions, and AI activity before you add infrastructure or re-architect applications. Also now generally available as part of MongoDB 9.0 are Intelligent Workload Management, expanded Queryable Encryption capabilities, and the MongoDB Extension for Hibernate ORM.

  • Atlas Infinite 

    • Atlas Infinite is the largest architectural innovation for MongoDB Atlas ever. It was built for the reality of the agentic era, when demand is constant, unpredictable, and extreme. It absorbs bursts of traffic and scales from prototype to petabyte on the same high-performance foundation, so organizations never outgrow it.

  • Atlas Agent Engine

    • Atlas Agent Engine lets developers build, deploy, and govern agents with persistent memory, context, built-in guardrails, and state management. Teams move from prototype to production without stitching together custom state stores, guardrails, and data pipelines.

  • New Voyage AI models and capabilities

    • Voyage AI by MongoDB embedding models and rerankers run next to your operational data, so agents retrieve accurate context in one pipeline instead of several. Recent Voyage AI releases include the Rerank 3 series, voyage-code-4, a retrieval model tuned specifically for coding agents, and automated embedding in Atlas Vector Search.

And that only scratches the surface; for everything MongoDB has released, and for the latest product news and ways we’ve innovated on behalf of customers, see our What’s New page.

Building (for) the road ahead

To paraphrase MongoDB CEO Dev Ittycheria, we expect that the data layer will eventually become an integral part of every organization’s control plane. As software moves from systems of record to systems that act on their own, the data layer of the tech stack will become ever more important.

The customers I’ve been meeting say they no longer want software that explains what happened. They need software, and the technology they rely on, to keep pace with what's happening right now. MongoDB was built for this reality, and we can’t wait to see what’s next.

title: AI Demand is Constant, Unpredictable, and Extreme. MongoDB is Built for It.
summary:
When a huge surge in demand meets limited resources, an awful experience usually isn’t far behind. Fans feel it when trying to compete for concert tickets with bots and scalpers. Diners feel it when they try to get a reservation at a trendy restaurant that’s fully booked for months. Websites and applications feel it when they go viral and get an accidental DDoS from a “Reddit Hug of Death.”

Unpredictable spikes in demand are only becoming more common, and scaling resources to meet them is hard. In my lifetime, I’ve seen big shifts in the amount of demand systems need to handle. First, the internet era, then the cloud era, we saw increased demand that was often predictable. Think of an annual flash sale or regular seasonality. Things might speed up, with more frequent spikes, but they were still spikes you could plan around.

Then AI happened. And this is where we live now: demand that’s constant, unpredictable, and extreme, increasing in frequency and intensity at the same time. If the internet era taught customers to expect an instant response, then the AI era is teaching them to expect something else: instant value. You can snap a photo of something you want, and an agent can identify it, buy it, and have it on your doorstep tomorrow. Those capabilities cut both ways. Change now hits every layer underneath faster and harder than before. The user isn't only human anymore. Agents are in the product too.

Agents don’t ease in. The second they’re on, they hit your system with massive, simultaneous reads and writes. They also take in and act on more information at once than any team of people ever could. Enterprises need a data layer built for that reality, where the only predictable thing is how unpredictable the load will be. Teams that can scale into those spikes will be the ones that last.

Introducing Atlas Infinite

Today, we're announcing Atlas Infinite, the largest architectural innovation for MongoDB Atlas ever. Atlas Infinite is purpose-built to handle the speed of development and unpredictable demand of applications that customers expect, with independent scaling of compute and storage to absorb sudden bursts of traffic.

Atlas Infinite is not a new database. It's a new deployment option within Atlas. Same document model, same drivers and APIs, no code changes required. Also, the current deployment option you know and love as MongoDB Atlas is not going anywhere. It just has a new name, MongoDB Atlas Core. Atlas Core and Atlas Infinite are the two database deployment options within the Atlas platform. You pick the right one for each workload.

How does Atlas Infinite deal with four key scaling and future-proofing problems organizations are dealing with today?

  1. Scaling delay: Gone. Atlas Infinite cuts read scaling time by more than 96% compared to Atlas Core. Compute and storage automatically scale independently within minutes, not hours.

  2. Storage ceiling: 10x higher. Atlas Infinite grows with you, from prototype to a petabyte, on the same foundation. You scale on your terms, when you need more performance, not when you run out of room. Atlas Infinite supports replica sets that hold 10x the data of replica sets in Atlas Core. 

  3. Capacity planning: No more guesswork. Atlas Infinite meets your needs in real time as you scale up and down. Atlas Infinite also runs more efficiently on the same hardware compared to Atlas Core, so you get nearly triple the performance per dollar.

  4. Re-architecture: Not required. Zero application changes required. Enjoy more elasticity and scalability on literally the same database.

This isn't only a scalability story. It's a more capable, more performant engine. Internal tests* using MongoDB 9.0 have shown that Atlas Infinite provides 189% more throughput per dollar compared with Atlas Core. And customers like Icon Solutions are using it to drive more growth.

"Atlas Infinite let us process 55% more transactions per second than our equivalent previous setup on MongoDB 8.0, with zero application changes. In payments, that kind of headroom without a re-architecture means faster, more reliable experiences for the customers on the other end of every transaction," said Mike Wallis, Head of DevOps at Icon Solutions.

Atlas Infinite is available as a public preview, and I can’t wait for you to try out the next generation of MongoDB Atlas.

MongoDB 9.0: The best version of MongoDB ever

In addition, we just released the best version of MongoDB ever, MongoDB 9.0. We’ve hardened the core to ensure a rock-solid foundation for the most demanding enterprises, and we’re setting a new bar for security, durability, availability, and performance.

That bar was already high. MongoDB 8.0 was released just two years ago, and today, nearly 80% of our Atlas fleet has adopted it, with higher customer satisfaction and stronger retention among these customers.

We are proud of what 8.0 delivered, and 9.0 pushes further still. Here are some of my favorite enhancements in MongoDB 9.0.

Performance*: 

  • In our internal tests against MongoDB 8.0, MongoDB 9.0 delivers:

    • Up to 35% faster find-one queries

    • Up to 30% faster update-one queries

    • Up to 2x throughput on large instances

    • Up to 20% higher throughput for transactional workloads

Security:

  • Queryable Encryption now supports prefix, suffix, and substring searches, allowing organizations to query sensitive information without ever decrypting it. 

  • Expanded private networking capabilities make it easier to deploy MongoDB Atlas securely across complex enterprise environments.

Durability and Availability:

  • Intelligent Workload Management automatically protects clusters when they are overloaded with requests and ensures short-running operations continue when demand is unpredictable.

  • Enhanced backup, restore, and recovery capabilities help organizations to maintain application availability and speed recovery when disruptions occur.

Observability & Developer Productivity:

  • Expanded observability into application and database performance

  • New developer productivity features that make it easier to modernize applications with familiar tools and frameworks, without costly rewrites.

MongoDB 9.0 continues to give you the freedom to run anywhere. MongoDB 9.0 is available in MongoDB Atlas and in self-managed environments through MongoDB Enterprise Advanced and MongoDB Community Edition.

MongoDB 9.0 on Atlas Infinite changes the calculus on scale. It's not something you plan around anymore, it's just there when you need it. There's never been a better time to build on MongoDB.

*Performance results are based on internal MongoDB testing comparing MongoDB 9.0 and MongoDB 8.0 using public benchmark methodologies. Results may vary by workload, deployment, hardware, and configuration.

title: Agentic Treasury: How AI Agents Turn Cash Blind Spots Into Real-Time, Governed Action
summary:
At 8 a.m., a $4 million payroll is due, but an expected customer payment hasn’t arrived. Leafy International’s treasury agent spots the gap in live payment data. It checks current balances and recommends a cash sweep from an overnight deposit. It’s enough to fund payroll while keeping Leafy’s $1 million minimum cash buffer intact.

Just as the treasurer reviews the proposal, an approved, time-stamped market feed flags a material EUR/USD move after a central bank announcement. The agent connects the signal to Leafy’s upcoming euro payment, refreshes the exposure, and flags it for review. A market alert is a reason to reassess, not permission to trade.

The treasurer views the rationale, data source, and update time, and then approves or delegates within the agreed mandate. If a balance, payment status, or foreign exchange (FX) rate changes before execution, the agent checks again. This is agentic treasury: Monitoring relevant conditions, recommending next steps, and helping carry them out only when authorized.

Leafy International is fictional, but the pressures and actions are real. Treasury teams are exploring how AI can improve decisions across payments, cash, working capital, and financial risk—and how to govern these systems.

Agentic treasury has two key requirements:

  • Context that stays current as balances, payments, and markets move

  • An independent check that confirms each action is authorized before it runs.

MongoDB provides the data layer for both, keeping the agent's context fresh as conditions change, and holding the controls and audit log that decide what the agent is allowed to do.

The industry shift to AI action

Cash and liquidity optimization remain persistent challenges for treasury teams. Nearly two-thirds of people surveyed by AFP cite cash management and forecasting as a top priority, while nearly 50% say they’re concerned about liquidity and cash planning.
